topics.title: Force, and balanced and unbalanced forces

concepts.label: The Concept of Force
concepts.cardText: A force can make an object move from rest, change the speed and direction of motion of a moving object, and can even change the shape of an object. Force is a physical quantity for which we need to specify direction along with its magnitude and unit, like position, displacement, velocity and acceleration. The SI unit of force is the newton, written with a small n, with the symbol N, and the magnitude of the force expresses its strength. If either the magnitude or direction, or both, of a force applied on an object changes, the effect of the force also changes. A spring balance can be used to measure the weight of an object, which is the gravitational force with which the Earth pulls the object, and more generally the magnitude of a force.

concepts.label: Balanced and Unbalanced Forces; Net Force
concepts.cardText: In real life usually more than one force acts on an object: when you push a box, the force of friction also acts on it in the direction opposite to its motion, and a ball floating on water has the gravitational force downwards and the buoyant force upwards. Two forces that are equal in magnitude but opposite in direction are called balanced forces; in a tug of war the rope does not move if the forces are balanced but moves if they are unbalanced. If the forces on an object are not balanced, a non-zero net force acts on it. When two forces are opposite in direction but unequal in magnitude, the magnitude of the net force is the difference between the magnitudes and its direction is along the larger force. When two forces act in the same direction, the net force is the sum of the magnitudes in the same direction. Multiple forces may act on an object, but its motion depends only on the net force.

concepts.label: The Force of Friction
concepts.cardText: When you push an object kept at rest on the floor, it may not move because of the force of friction arising between the bottom surface of the box and the floor, acting in a direction opposite to the force you apply. The box starts moving when the force applied is larger than the force of friction, so that a net force acts on the box in the direction of its motion. Other forces on a pushed object are the gravitational force (weight), acting downwards, and the force exerted by the surface on which it is placed, called the normal force, acting upwards perpendicular to the surface; these two are balanced. Air around the object also exerts friction, but in many cases it is so small it can be neglected. A moving object such as a bicycle or ball comes to rest after some distance because the force of friction acts against the direction of motion; to keep an object moving we must continuously apply a force to counter friction.

concepts.label: Friction Depends on the Surfaces: Coins and Spring Balance Activities
concepts.cardText: In Activity 6.1 a stack of coins is released by a stretched rubber band on surfaces of different materials, and its velocity decreases gradually until it comes to rest. Before release it is stationary, so the forces on it are balanced. On release the force from the stretched rubber band is larger than the force of friction, so a net force acts forward and gives an acceleration in the forward direction. When the coins lose contact with the rubber band, only the force of friction continues to act in the direction opposite to their motion, gradually decreasing the velocity and bringing them to rest. Even though the rubber band is stretched by the same amount each time, the distance travelled on different surfaces changes, which indicates that the force of friction on these surfaces is different. In Activity 6.2 the reading of a spring balance gives an approximate measure of the force of friction: a smaller reading means a smaller force of friction. When the force of friction is smaller, the velocity of the stack decreases more slowly and it travels a larger distance before coming to rest.

concepts.label: Galileo, Thought Experiments and Inertia
concepts.cardText: In ancient times it was well recognised that a force was required to move a stationary object or to stop a moving object. But for ages it was mistakenly thought that a force was also required to keep an object moving with a constant velocity. Only in the 17th century did Galileo Galilei argue, through a series of thought experiments, that if a body moves along a horizontal plane and all impediments to its motion are removed, it will continue to move indefinitely. A thought experiment is done when the conditions required for the experiment are difficult to recreate in the real world, for example imagining an object and a floor so smooth that the force of friction between them is zero. Isaac Newton used the word inertia to describe the tendency of objects to resist change in their state of rest or uniform motion, and used this idea to frame his first law of motion; along with it he presented two more laws of motion in 1687.

concepts.label: Newton's First Law of Motion
concepts.cardText: Newton's first law of motion states that an object at rest remains at rest, and an object in motion continues to move with a constant velocity, unless a net force acts upon the object. In other words, if the net force acting on an object is zero, the body cannot begin to move or change its velocity, and its acceleration is zero. An object at rest has zero velocity, and constant velocity means no change in the magnitude or the direction of velocity. If a person pushes a moving box with a force equal to the force of friction, the two forces balance, the net force is zero, and the box continues moving with constant velocity. When no net force is acting, either the object is at rest or it moves with a constant velocity. If the force of friction were zero, a net force would be needed to set an object at rest moving, but once moving no further force would be required to keep it moving with a constant velocity; to change the velocity or stop a moving object, a force must be applied.

concepts.label: Force, Mass and Acceleration: Newton's Second Law
concepts.cardText: A force can set an object in motion, bring it to rest, or change its velocity; a change in velocity means the object is accelerating, so a force produces acceleration. In Activity 6.3 a cart is pulled by a cup of weights through a thread over a pulley; doubling the force on the same mass of the cart increases the acceleration, so the acceleration of an object of fixed mass increases as the net force applied on it increases. In Activity 6.4 the mass of the cart is doubled with the same force and the acceleration decreases, so for a given magnitude of force the acceleration produced is inversely related to the mass of the object. Newton's second law of motion states that when a net force acts on an object, the object accelerates in the direction of the net force; the magnitude of the acceleration is proportional to the magnitude of the net force and inversely proportional to the mass of the object, written F = ma, and the direction of acceleration is the same as the direction of the net force. One newton is defined as the force that produces an acceleration of 1 m per second squared on an object of mass 1 kg. In practice, the measured change may be a little less than expected because of friction between the cart's wheels and the surface and measurement errors.

concepts.label: Gravitational Force and Weight
concepts.cardText: Under the influence of the gravitational force an object falls towards the Earth, and the acceleration involved is called the acceleration due to the gravitational force by the Earth, denoted by g, with the same unit as acceleration. Using the second law, the gravitational force on an object of mass m is mg. The value of g is 9.8 m per second squared and can be taken to be nearly constant near the surface of the Earth; for quick estimations 10 m per second squared can be used. The acceleration due to gravity does not depend on the mass of the object. A force of 1 N is around the upward force your palm applies on a 100 g mass held in it. In Example 6.4 a barbell of total mass 30 kg has a downward gravitational force of 294 N, so to keep it steady the weightlifter applies an equal force of 294 N in the opposite, upward, direction.

concepts.label: Reducing Force by Increasing Time: Catching, Airbags and Coconuts
concepts.cardText: A cricket fielder catching a fast ball gradually pulls their hands backwards with the ball after catching it. This increases the time during which the high velocity of the ball reduces to zero, which reduces the magnitude of the acceleration of the ball, so a smaller force is needed to stop it, which also minimises injury to the fielder. Airbags in vehicles work for a similar reason: in a collision the airbag inflates quickly into a soft compressible cushion, and the passenger's head and chest push into the bag instead of hitting the hard steering wheel or dashboard, so the time over which the hitting occurs increases. Smaller acceleration means a reduced force on the person, lowering the risk of serious injuries, particularly with seat belt use. In cracking a coconut, the coconut hits a hard surface and stops in a very short time; to change its velocity so quickly the ground must exert a very large force, which breaks the shell.

concepts.label: Newton's Third Law of Motion
concepts.cardText: At least two objects must interact for a force to come into play: when you push a ball with your foot you feel a force applied by the ball on your foot. In Activity 6.5, pushing a heavy table while sitting on a wheeled chair makes you move in the opposite direction, and pulling the table moves you the other way; each time you apply a force on the table, the table applies a force on you in the opposite direction. In Activity 6.6 two spring balances connected hook to hook and pulled in opposite directions show the same readings every time, indicating that the forces they apply on each other are equal in magnitude. Newton's third law of motion states that whenever one object is exerting a force on a second object, the second object is simultaneously exerting an equal and opposite force on the first object. The forces always occur in pairs but these two forces act on two different objects. A pair of equal and opposite forces acts on two different objects, so they do not balance each other; if two equal and opposite forces act on the same object, they balance each other.

concepts.label: Friction Helps Us Walk
concepts.cardText: To move forward on a bicycle without pedalling you push the ground backwards with your feet, and the ground pushes your feet in the opposite direction, so both you and the bicycle move forward. This is how we walk or run: we push the ground backwards with our feet and the ground applies an opposite force, in the form of friction, to make us move forward. In this case friction helps us move rather than oppose us. When the foot tries to slide backwards the force of friction acts in the forward direction; without friction the foot would slip backwards and we would fall down. Grooves on the soles of footwear and treads on tyres increase the force of friction with the floor and road. That is why it is difficult to walk on wet polished floors or ice, and risky to drive on roads covered with water or snow.

concepts.label: The Third Law at Work: Canoe, Balloon and Rocket
concepts.cardText: A person climbing a coconut tree pushes down against the trunk and the friction between the trunk and the legs pushes the person upwards by an equal force, so it is harder to climb smooth trunks that have less friction. When a canoeist pushes the water backwards with the paddle, the water pushes the paddle forward with an equal force; the two forces are equal but act on different objects, the paddle and the water, so they do not cancel, and the force on the paddle moves the paddle and canoe forward. When the canoeist pushes harder the forward force is larger and the canoe's velocity increases. In the balloon activity the stretched balloon pushes the air out and the air rushing out exerts an equal force on the balloon in the opposite direction, so the balloon moves opposite to the air. A rocket engine produces gas and expels it downward, which exerts an equal and opposite upward force on the rocket; when this is larger than the weight of the rocket the net force is upward and the rocket lifts off. Firing the engine in the direction of motion slows the rocket, as the Vikram lander of Chandrayaan-3 did.

concepts.label: Third Law for All Forces; Equal Forces, Unequal Accelerations
concepts.cardText: Newton's third law applies to all types of forces, contact or non-contact, that we come across in everyday mechanical situations: two bar magnets apply equal and opposite magnetic forces on each other, two similarly charged balloons apply equal and opposite electrostatic forces, and the Earth and a fruit apply equal and opposite gravitational forces on each other. Though the forces on the Earth and the fruit are equal in magnitude, the mass of the Earth is so large that the acceleration of the Earth caused by the force is extremely small and its effect is too small to be noticed. In Example 6.8, when a 0.1 kg bullet is fired from a 5 kg gun the recoil force on the gun is equal to the force on the bullet, but the accelerations are not equal because their masses are different. Even though the forces on two interacting objects are always equal in magnitude they do not, in general, produce equal accelerations, because the masses of the objects may be different.

topics.title: Forces on a system of objects

concepts.label: Forces Acting on a System of Objects
concepts.cardText: Newton's laws can be applied to two or more objects connected together. For two boxes connected by a string on a frictionless horizontal surface, with a force F pulling Box 1, Box 1 applies a force on Box 2 via the string, and by the third law Box 2 applies an equal and opposite force on Box 1; this force is called tension T. One approach is to calculate the net force on each box separately and then use the second law; a simpler way is to consider the two boxes and the string as a single system. In that approach the forces within the system (internal forces) need not be considered and only forces that act from the outside (external forces) matter: the tension T is the internal force and F is the external force. The system of two boxes accelerates just like a single object of mass m1 + m2. Treating connected objects as a system often simplifies the analysis, and gravitational force on the system is balanced by the normal force from the ground.
